name: Kabīr

tradition.text: 1398–1518 (a life of 120 years); in the Kabīr Panth, Kabīr appeared as an infant on a lotus in Lahartārā tank and was found by the weavers Nīrū and Nīmā

scholarly.text: c. 1440–1518 on the common view; Ch. Vaudeville argued 1398–1448

realization_account.text: Initiated by Rāmānanda, who stumbled on him lying on the steps of the Pañcagaṅgā ghāṭ before dawn and uttered 'Rām' (Rāmānandī and popular account); in the Kabīr Panth he needs no guru, being the Sat Puruṣ himself, and accepts Rāmānanda only to model discipleship. At his death at Maghar his Hindu and Muslim followers disputed his body; under the shroud they found only flowers, which they divided for a samādhi and a tomb.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Weaver (julāhā) poet-saint of Banaras, raised in a Muslim weaver household, the most influential of the Sants: he taught love of the formless Rām through the Name and the true guru, mocked the formalism of paṇḍit and mullā, yogī and ascetic, rejected caste, idols and pilgrimage, and spoke of the natural state (sahaj) and of dying while alive. His words survive in three recensions (the eastern Bījak, the Rajasthani Granthāvalī/Pañcvāṇī, the Punjabi Ādi Granth) and in a vast oral corpus; the Kabīr Panth reveres him as the incarnate True Being.
notes: Relation to Rāmānanda is disputed (dsp:kabir-guru-ramananda). Encounters with Sikandar Lodī and with Gorakhnāth are legendary.

name: Ravidās (Raidās)

tradition.text: born 1377 (Ravidāsī reckoning; birth celebrated on Māgh Pūrṇimā) and very long-lived

realization_account.text: Rāmānanda's disciple in the Rāmānandī account; the brahmins who challenged his right to worship were defeated by signs (the image came to his lap; Gaṅgā appeared in his leather-soaking bowl); the queen Jhālī of Chittor and Mīrābāī became his disciples.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Leatherworker (Camār) saint of Banaras, venerated as Guru Ravidās: his songs speak of the city without sorrow (Begampura), of God who raises the lowly, of his own despised caste without shame, and of the unity of self and God. Forty of his hymns are in the Ādi Granth; the Ravidāsī community reveres him as its guru.
notes: Mīrābāī's discipleship rests on her songs naming Raidās as guru (attribution debated).

name: Dādū Dayāl

tradition.text: 1544–1603; found floating on the Sābarmatī by the Nāgar brahmin Lodīrām (panth account)

scholarly.text: 1544–1603, probably born into a Muslim cotton-carder family

realization_account.text: At eleven, an old man (Buḍḍhan, 'the old one'; some say Kabīr or God himself) appeared to him, gave him pān and blessed him; seven years later he appeared again and Dādū's realization was complete; he met the guru 'in the unseen' (gaib).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Cotton-carder (dhuniyā) saint of Rajasthan, founder of the Dādū Panth: taught remembrance of the one Rām of Hindu and Turk, impartiality (nipakh), the body as the true mosque and temple, and dying to self; met Akbar at Fatehpur Sikri (1585).

name: Buḍḍhan (Vṛddhānanda)
summary: The old man who appeared to the boy Dādū and blessed him, counted as Dādū's guru; identified by some in the panth with Kabīr or with God.

name: Pīpā
summary: Rajput king of Gāgraun who renounced his throne to become a disciple of Rāmānanda and a wandering devotee with his wife Sītā; one hymn in the Ādi Granth ('the body is the temple, the body is the pilgrim').

name: Sain (Sen) the barber
summary: Barber devotee counted among Rāmānanda's disciples, remembered for Hari taking his place in service to the king; a hymn in the Ādi Granth.

name: Dhannā
summary: Jat farmer devotee of Rajasthan counted among Rāmānanda's disciples; the story of the stone that ate his offering; hymns in the Ādi Granth.

name: Sadhnā the butcher
summary: Muslim butcher devotee whose hymn in the Ādi Granth is among the bhagat-bāṇī; named by Ravidās among those the Lord saved.

name: Dharamdās

scholarly.text: 16th c. (if historical); the Dharamdāsī texts in his name are later

summary: Wealthy merchant (of Bāndhavgaṛh) who became Kabīr's chief disciple; the Anurāg Sāgar is Kabīr's teaching to him; his line of forty-two generations of ācāryas leads the Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth.

name: Cūṛāmaṇi Nām (Muktāmaṇi Nām)
summary: Son of Dharamdās, first of the forty-two ācāryas (vaṃś) of the Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth.

name: Surat Gopāl
summary: Disciple of Kabīr to whom the Kabīr Chaurā line of Varanasi traces its succession of mahants.

name: Bhāgodās (Bhagvān Dās)
summary: Disciple of Kabīr credited by the panth with compiling the Bījak.

name: Kamāl
summary: Kabīr's son (or adopted son) in the legends, himself a devotee to whom some verses are ascribed; the proverb 'Kabīr's line sank when the son Kamāl was born' is quoted against him.

name: Pūran Sāhib
summary: Kabīr Panth teacher of Burhanpur, author of the Bījak commentary Trijyā that founded the 'pārakh' (discernment) reading of the Bījak.

name: Viśvanāth Siṃh of Rewā
summary: Mahārāj of Rewā, author of the Pākhaṇḍ-khaṇḍinī commentary on the Bījak.

name: Anantadās
summary: Rāmānandī hagiographer (disciple in the line of Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī) who wrote the Paracaīs of Kabīr, Raidās, Pīpā, Nāmdev and others.

name: Jhālī Rānī of Chittor
summary: Queen of Chittor who, in the Ravidāsī and Rāmānandī hagiographies, became Ravidās's disciple and invited him to her court.

name: Sant Sarwan Dass
summary: Head of Dera Sachkhand Ballan (Jalandhar) who shaped the modern Ravidāsī dera tradition.

name: Sant Niranjan Dass
summary: Head of Dera Sachkhand Ballan under whom the Ravidassia Dharam and the Amritbāṇī were declared (2010).

name: Mangu Ram Mugowalia
summary: Founder of the Ād Dharm movement in Punjab (1925), which declared the Ravidāsī Dalits a distinct religious community.

name: Garībdās (son of Dādū)
summary: Dādū's elder son and first successor at Naraina.

name: Miskīndās
summary: Dādū's younger son, a poet of the Dādū Panth.

name: Rajjab
summary: Pathan disciple of Dādū who, on his way to his wedding in the groom's crown, met Dādū and renounced, wearing the crown for life; arranged the Dādū Vāṇī in aṅgas and compiled the Sarbaṅgī anthology.

name: Sundardās (the younger)
summary: Dādū's learned disciple, a Khaṇḍelvāl Vaiśya of Dausa who studied Sanskrit at Banaras; the most scholarly Sant poet, author of Jñān Samudra and Sundar Vilās, joining Sant bhakti with yoga and Advaita.

name: Jangopāl
summary: Disciple of Dādū and author of the Dādū Janma Līlā.

name: Bakhnā
summary: Disciple of Dādū and poet of the Dādū Panth.

name: Gopāldās (Dādūpanthī)
summary: Compiler of the Sarvāṅgī of 1627.

name: Malūkdās
summary: Sant of Kaṛā (near Allahabad), known for trust in providence ('Malūkdās says: Rām is the giver of all') and for teaching the inner Rām beyond sect.

name: Paltū Sāhib
summary: Sant of Ayodhyā (born near Jalālpur), fierce critic of hypocrisy and exponent of the inner Name and sound; a Sant Mat authority.

name: Dariyā Sāhib of Bihar
summary: Sant of Dharkandhā (Shahabad, Bihar), founder of a Dariyā panth, teacher of the Name and the inner regions.

name: Dariyāv Sāhib of Mārvāṛ
summary: Sant of Rain (Marwar), founder of the Rain seat of the Rāmsnehīs.

name: Caraṇdās

realization_account.text: As a boy he met the sage Śukadeva in the forest and received initiation; he then practised yoga and devotion for years before teaching.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Delhi Sant, founder of the Caraṇdāsī sampradāya, who joined nirguṇa teaching with Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa devotion and aṣṭāṅga yoga; his guru was Śukadeva, who appeared to him.

name: Sahajobāī
summary: Woman Sant, disciple of Caraṇdās, author of the Sahaj Prakāś, famous for placing the guru above Hari.

name: Dayābāī
summary: Woman Sant, disciple (and kinswoman) of Caraṇdās, author of the Dayā Bodh.

name: Garībdās of Chhuḍānī

realization_account.text: Kabīr appeared to him in the fields at the age of ten and showed him Satlok.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Jat householder Sant of Haryana who at ten met Kabīr in person and thereafter declared him the supreme God; founder of the Garībdāsī panth.

name: Jagjīvandās
summary: Kṣatriya Sant of Koṭvā (Barabanki), founder of the Satnāmī sampradāya of Awadh.

name: Bīrbhān
summary: Founder (1657) of the Satnāmīs of Narnaul, whose community rose against Aurangzeb in 1672.

name: Ghāsīdās
summary: Founder of the Satnāmī panth of Chhattisgarh among the Camārs: rejected images and caste, enjoined vegetarianism and abstinence, and taught the true name.

name: Haridās Nirañjanī
summary: Founder of the Nirañjanī sampradāya of Rajasthan, who joined Nāth yoga and Sant devotion to Nirañjan.

name: Rāmcaraṇ
summary: Founder of the Shāhpurā Rāmsnehīs, author of the Aṇbhai Vāṇī.

name: Tulsī Sāhib of Hāthras

tradition.text: he said he had been Tulsīdās in a former birth

summary: Sant of Hāthras, author of the Ghaṭ Rāmāyaṇ, whose teaching of the inner regions and sound current directly preceded Radhasoami; Soamiji's family were among his followers.
notes: Whether Tulsī Sāhib was Soamiji's guru is disputed within Sant Mat.

name: Bhīkhā Sāhib
summary: Sant of the Bāvrī line (Bhurkuḍā, Ghazipur) whose verses are printed in the Santbānī series.

name: Gulāl Sāhib
summary: Sant of the Bāvrī line at Bhurkuḍā, teacher of Bhīkhā Sāhib.

name: Bāvrī Sāhibā
summary: Woman Sant of Delhi to whom the Bāvrī line of Sants (Yārī, Bullā, Gulāl, Bhīkhā) traces itself.

name: Shiv Dayal Singh (Soamiji Maharaj)

realization_account.text: He practised surat-śabd yoga in a back room for some fifteen years before opening satsang to the public in 1861.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Khatri of Agra who, after years of inner practice, opened public satsang on Basant Pañcamī 1861 and founded Radhasoami; his discourses and poems are the Sār Bachan.

name: Rai Salig Ram (Huzur Maharaj)
summary: Postmaster-General of the North-Western Provinces and Soamiji's leading disciple, who systematized Radhasoami doctrine and led the Agra satsang.

name: Partap Singh (Chachaji Maharaj)
summary: Soamiji's younger brother, associated with the Soamibagh line.

name: Radhaji (Narayani Devi)
summary: Soamiji's wife, revered in the Agra satsang; one account derives the name 'Radhasoami' from 'Radha' and 'Soami'.

name: Brahm Shankar Misra (Maharaj Saheb)
summary: Successor of Rai Salig Ram in the Agra line, author of Discourses on Radhasoami Faith.

name: Kamta Prasad Sinha (Sarkar Sahab)
summary: Agra-line guru of Ghazipur, predecessor of Anand Swarup in the Dayalbagh succession.

name: Anand Swarup (Sahabji Maharaj)
summary: Founder of the Dayalbagh colony at Agra (1915), joining Radhasoami practice with industry, education and community life.

name: Jaimal Singh (Baba Ji Maharaj)
summary: Sikh soldier and disciple of Soamiji who settled at Beas (1891) and founded the Beas line.

name: Sawan Singh (Huzur Maharaj)
summary: Army engineer and Jaimal Singh's successor at Beas (1903–1948), who spread Sant Mat to India and the West; author of Gurmat Siddhānt and Spiritual Gems.

name: Jagat Singh (Sardar Bahadur Maharaj)
summary: Chemistry professor, Master at Beas 1948–1951.

name: Charan Singh (Maharaj Charan Singh)
summary: Master at Beas 1951–1990, grandson of Sawan Singh, author of Die to Live and many discourses.

name: Gurinder Singh Dhillon (Baba Gurinder Singh)
summary: Master at Beas from 1990.

name: Julian P. Johnson
summary: American surgeon and disciple of Sawan Singh, author of The Path of the Masters (1939).

name: Kirpal Singh
summary: Disciple of Sawan Singh who founded Ruhani Satsang in Delhi (1951) and taught widely in the West; author of Naam or Word and The Crown of Life.

name: Darshan Singh
summary: Son of Kirpal Singh; founded the Sawan Kirpal Ruhani Mission (1974); Urdu poet.

name: Rajinder Singh
summary: Successor of Darshan Singh; head of Science of Spirituality / Sawan Kirpal Ruhani Mission from 1989.

name: Thakar Singh
summary: Disciple of Kirpal Singh who led a separate line after 1976.

name: Ajaib Singh (Sant Ji)
summary: Disciple of Kirpal Singh, teacher at Sant Bani Ashram (77 RB, Rajasthan), associated with the English Anurāg Sāgar.

name: Maharshi Mehi Paramhans
summary: Bihar Santmat master, author of the Satsaṅg Yog, teacher of a graded practice of repetition, form, point and sound.

name: Lalon Fakir (Lālan Sāṃi)

tradition.text: his followers say he lived 116 years; birth variously 1772 or 1774

scholarly.text: died 17 October 1890 at Cheuṛiyā; birth unknown (c. 1770s by most reports)

realization_account.text: Abandoned by his companions on a pilgrimage when he fell ill with smallpox, he was nursed by a Muslim household and met his guru Sirāj Sāṃi; his caste of birth (Hindu Kāyastha or Muslim) was lost and he himself refused to name it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The greatest Bāul master, of Cheuṛiyā near Kushtia: his songs of the unknown bird in the body's cage, the Man of the Heart, the mirror-city, the futility of caste and creed and the worship of the human are the classic Bāul teaching. His disciples ('Lalon's fakirs') keep his ākhṛā and festival.
notes: Birth, origin (Hindu or Muslim) and the details of the smallpox story are disputed; flagged recent because his life extends to 1890.

name: Sirāj Sāṃi
summary: Fakir (a palanquin-bearer by some accounts) who was Lalon's guru; named in the signature (bhaṇitā) of Lalon's songs.

name: Duddu Śāh
summary: Disciple of Lalon and composer of Bāul songs; wrote a verse life of Lalon (low confidence).

name: Bholāi Śāh
summary: Disciple of Lalon who continued his ākhṛā.

name: Maniruddin Śāh
summary: Disciple of Lalon (low confidence).

name: Pāñju Śāh
summary: Fakir-Bāul poet of Jhenaidah whose songs of mārephat (gnosis) and the body are widely sung.

name: Pāglā Kānāi
summary: Bāul-Fakir singer-poet of Jhenaidah famed for extempore songs and song-debates (kabigān style).

name: Gagan Harkarā
summary: Postal runner of Shilaidaha whose song 'āmi kothāy pāba tāre, āmār maner mānuṣ ye re' Rabindranath Tagore admired and whose tune he adapted.

name: Madan Bāul
summary: Bāul known through Rabindranath Tagore's quotation of his song 'your path is hidden by temple and mosque'.

name: Kāṅgāl Harināth (Harināth Majumdar)
summary: Journalist of Kumarkhali (Grāmbārtā Prakāśikā) and composer of Bāul-style songs as 'Phikir Cāṃd'; acquainted with Lalon.

name: Hāsan Rājā
summary: Zamindar-poet of Sunamganj (Sylhet) whose mystic songs of detachment are sung with the Bāul repertoire.

name: Rādhāraman Datta
summary: Vaiṣṇava mystic poet of Sylhet (dhāmāil songs of Rādhā's longing), close to the Sahajiyā and Bāul idiom.

name: Jālāl Khān (Jālāl Uddin Khān)
summary: Mymensingh mystic poet whose songs (Jālāl Gītikā) treat the body, the human and the one God in the Bāul-Fakir idiom.

name: Śāh Ābdul Karim
summary: Sylheti Bāul singer-poet, called Bāul Samrāṭ, whose songs join mystic longing and social protest.

name: Nabanī Dās Khyāpā Bāul
summary: Birbhum Bāul known to Rabindranath Tagore at Santiniketan; father of Pūrṇa Dās.

name: Pūrṇa Dās Bāul
summary: Bāul singer of Birbhum who carried Bāul song to world audiences.

name: Sanātan Dās Bāul
summary: Bankura Bāul master (Khayerbuni ākhṛā), respected as a sādhaka-singer of the older style.

name: Bhabā Pāglā
summary: Mystic singer-poet of Bengal (Kalna) whose songs to the Mother and the Man of the Heart are sung by Bāuls.

name: Muhammad Mansuruddin
summary: Collector of Bengali folk songs (Hārāmaṇi), a principal preserver of Lalon's and other Bāul songs in print.
notes: A collector and scholar, not a Bāul teacher; recorded because the written transmission of the songs depends on him.

name: Caṇḍīdās (the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās)

tradition.text: before Caitanya, who is said to have delighted in his songs; placed at Nānnur (Birbhum) or Chhātnā (Bankura)

scholarly.text: the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās padas are 16th–18th c.; distinct from Baḍu Caṇḍīdās of the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan

realization_account.text: A priest of Bāśulī, he loved the washerwoman Rāmī; Sahajiyā tradition makes their love the exemplary practice of prema.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The Bengali poet whom the Sahajiyās claim as their master: lover of the washerwoman Rāmī, singer of the love of man above all; one of several poets called Caṇḍīdās.
notes: The 'Caṇḍīdās problem': several poets used the name; U26 owns Caṇḍīdās as a Vaiṣṇava poet.

name: Rāmī (Rajakinī)
summary: The washerwoman whom the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās loved; revered by Sahajiyās as the model female partner, to whom some songs are attributed.

name: Mukunda Dāsa (Sahajiyā)
summary: Sahajiyā teacher to whom the Amṛtaratnāvalī and Bhṛṅgaratnāvalī are attributed; claimed by Sahajiyās as a disciple of Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja.

name: Akiñcana Dāsa
summary: Author of the Vivartavilāsa, which reads the Caitanya-caritāmṛta as Sahajiyā doctrine.

name: Rūpa Kavirāja
summary: Gauḍīya teacher who taught that in rāgānugā practice the rules of vaidhī bhakti may be abandoned; condemned by Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and remembered in Gauḍīya accounts as a deviant close to Sahajiyā views.

name: Āulcānd

tradition.text: appeared c. 1694 (tradition); departed in the later 18th c.

realization_account.text: Caitanya, who had disappeared at Puri, reappeared in Bengal as Āulcānd to reveal the secret sahaja religion to the poor and low-caste.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The mysterious founder of the Kartābhajā, who appeared as a youth in a betel garden at Ulā (Nadia), was held to be Caitanya returned, wandered with twenty-two disciples, and chose Rāmśaraṇ Pāl as his successor.

name: Rāmśaraṇ Pāl
summary: Sadgop householder of Ghoshpara, chief disciple of Āulcānd and first Kartā; organized the Kartābhajā community.

name: Satī Mā (Sarasvatī)
summary: Wife of Rāmśaraṇ Pāl, revered as the Mother of the Kartābhajā, who led the community after her husband; her shrine and the pomegranate tree at Ghoshpara are healing sites.

name: Rāmdulāl Pāl (Dulālcānd)
summary: Son of Rāmśaraṇ and Satī Mā, Kartā of the sect and composer of the Bhāber Gīt; under him the sect expanded into Calcutta.

name: Manulāl Miśra
summary: Kartābhajā Mahāśay and author of the Sahajatattva-prakāśa (early 20th c.).

name: Balarām Hāḍi
summary: Founder of the Balarāmī sect of Meherpur, of the Hāḍi caste, venerated by his followers as God (Hāḍirām).

name: Kubir Gõsāi
summary: Poet of the Sāhebdhanī sect whose songs in the Sahajiyā-Bāul idiom are sung in Nadia.
